newsitem.title: USA: USDA looking into Egypt decree on biotech imports.
newsitem.headline: USDA looking into Egypt decree on biotech imports.

text.p: A senior U.S. Agriculture Department official Thursday said USDA was looking into an Egyptian order barring imports of genetically-altered commodities and had not yet been able to meet with government officials in Cairo because of a holiday.

"We're pressing for a meeting on Monday," Timothy Galvin, Associate Administrator at USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service. "We're not worried but very concerned and that's why we're trying to meet with Eyptian agriculture officials."

Egypt's Ministry of Health issued a decree, dated July 1, that imported grains and soybeans meant for human consumption must be accompanied by a certificate which proves genetic engineering was not used in their production.
Galvin said USDA was alerted to the decree by the U.S. grain industry on Wednesday and that so far it has not affected the flow of trade.
Galvin said the order also says "all imports of food stuff commodities produced by using genetically-engineered theories are prohibited until proved to be safe."

"We would go in and express very strong concerns about this," Galvin said. "We would also point out in fact these commodities and seeds they were produced from have been proven safe and approved under U.S. regulations."
The Clinton Administration has embraced genetically-altered crops as the best option for feeding a hungry world. U.S. farmers have planted them in great numbers because of high yields.
But the technology has been greeted with skepticism abroad.

The U.S. has clashed with the European Union over EU rules that call for labeling of foods made with biotech crops and demands by some EU activists that biotech crops be handled, stored and sold separately from other crops.
